title: Lucullus
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi046.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Nec vero satis constituere possum quod sit eorum consilium aut quid velint. interdum enim cum adhibemus ad eos orationem eius modi, si ea quae disputentur vera sint tum omnia fore incerta, respondent: quid ergo istud ad nos? num nostra culpa est? naturam accusa, quae in profundo veritatem ut ait Democritus penitus abstruserit. alii autem elegantius, qui etiam queruntur quod eos insimulemus omnia incerta dicere, quantumque intersit inter incertum et id quod percipi non possit docere conantur eaque distinguere.
passages.english: Nor indeed can I quite determine what their plan is or what they want. For sometimes, when we address to them an argument of this kind, that if the things they argue were true, then everything would be uncertain, they reply: "What is that to us, then? Is it our fault? Accuse nature, which, as Democritus says, has hidden truth deep down in the abyss." Others, however, [answer] more elegantly: they even complain that we charge them with saying that everything is uncertain, and they try to show how great a difference there is between the uncertain and that which cannot be perceived, and to distinguish them.

passages.original: deinde postulas ut, si mundus ita sit par alteri mundo ut inter eos ne minimum quidem intersit, concedatur tibi ut in hoc quoque nostro mundo aliquid alicui sic sit par ut nihil differat nihil intersit. cur enim inquies ex illis individuis, unde omnia Democritus gigni adfirmat, in reliquis mundis et in iis quidem innumerabilibus innumerabiles Q. Lutatii Catuli non modo possint esse sed etiam sint, in hoc tanto mundo Catulus alter non possit effici? Primum quiderm me ad Democritum vocas;
passages.english: Next you demand that, if one world is so equal to another world that there is not even the least difference between them, it be granted to you that in this world of ours too one thing is so equal to another that it differs in nothing and there is no difference at all. "For why," you will say, "when out of those indivisibles, from which Democritus asserts that all things are generated, in the other worlds, and those innumerable, innumerable Quintus Lutatius Catuluses not only can exist but actually do exist, can a second Catulus not be produced in this vast world?" First, then, you summon me to Democritus;

passages.original: sed quaerimus de sapiente. ego vero ipse et magnus quidam sum opinator (non enim sum sapiens) et meas cogitationes sic dirigo, non ad illam parvulam Cynosuram, qua fidunt duce nocturna Phoenices in alto, ut ait Aratus, eoque directius gubernant quod eam tenent quae cursu interiore brevi convertitur orbe — sed Helicen et clarissimos Septentriones id est rationes has latiore specie non ad tenue limatas; eo fit ut errem et vager latius.
passages.english: But we are inquiring about the wise man. I myself, indeed, am a great holder of opinions (for I am not wise), and I steer my thoughts not by that tiny Cynosura, "which the Phoenicians trust as their guide by night on the deep," as Aratus says, and steer the more directly because they keep to that which "turns in a short circle on an inner course" — but by Helice and the most brilliant Septentriones, that is, by these reasonings of broader aspect, not filed down to fineness; so it happens that I stray and wander more widely.
passages.notes: Cynosura is the Little Bear, Helice and the Septentriones the Great Bear.

passages.original: Et primum quod initio dixisti videamus quale sit, similiter a nobis de antiquis philosophis commemorari atque seditiosi solerent claros viros sed tamen populares aliquos nominare. illi cum res non bonas tractent similes bonorum videri volunt; nos autem ea dicimus nobis videri quae vosmet ipsi nobilissimis philosophis placuisse conceditis. Anaxagoras nivem nigram dixit esse. ferres me si ego idem dicerem? tu ne si dubitarem quidem. at quis est? num hic sophistes (sic enim appellabantur ii qui ostentationis aut quaestus causa philosophantur)? maxima fuit et gravitatis et ingeni gloria.
passages.english: And first let us see what sort of thing it is that you said at the beginning: that we cite the ancient philosophers in the same way that seditious men used to name certain famous men, but men of the popular party. They, though they handle things that are not good, want to seem like good men; we, however, say that those things seem [true] to us which you yourselves concede were approved by the noblest philosophers. Anaxagoras said that snow was black. Would you bear with me if I said the same? Not even if I [merely] doubted it. But who is he? Surely not a sophist (for that is what those were called who practise philosophy for display or for gain)? His was the greatest renown both for seriousness and for intellect.

passages.original: num ergo is excaecat nos aut orbat sensibus, si parum magnam vim censet in is esse ad ea quae sub eos subiecta sunt iudicanda? Parmenides Xenophanes minus bonis quamquam versibus sed tamen illi versibus increpant eorum adrogantiam quasi irati, qui cum sciri nihil possit audeant se scire dicere. Et ab iis aiebat removendum Socratem et Platonem cur, an de ullis certius possum dicere? vixisse cum iis equidem videor, ita multi sermones perscripti sunt e quibus dubitari non possit quin Socrati nihil sit visum sciri posse; excepit unum tantum, scire se nihil se scire, nihil amplius.
passages.english: Does he, then, blind us or rob us of our senses, if he thinks there is too little power in them for judging the things that are placed under them? Parmenides and Xenophanes, in verses less good, it is true, but verses nonetheless, rebuke, as if angry, the arrogance of those who, though nothing can be known, dare to say that they know. And you said Socrates and Plato should be set apart from these. Why? Or can I speak more certainly about anyone? I seem, indeed, to have lived with them, so many are the dialogues written down from which it cannot be doubted that Socrates thought nothing could be known; he excepted one thing only, that he knew that he knew nothing, nothing more.
passages.notes: 'Et ab iis aiebat removendum' is awkward; translated as 'you said' (Lucullus' argument). Some editors emend the passage.

passages.original: nam et in remo sentio non esse id quod videatur, et in columba pluris videri colores nec esse plus uno. deinde nihilne praeterea diximus? Maneant illa omnia; †lacerat ista causa; veracis suos esse sensus dicit Epicurus. Igitur semper auctorem habes, et eum qui magno suo periculo causam agat; eo enim rem demittit Epicurus, si unus sensus semel in vita mentitus sit, nulli umquam esse credendum.
passages.english: For in the case of the oar I perceive that what appears is not so, and in the case of the dove that more colours appear but there is not more than one. Next, did we say nothing beyond this? Let all those points stand; †this case tears [your position] apart†; Epicurus says his senses are truthful. So you always have an authority, and one who pleads the case at great risk to himself; for Epicurus brings the matter to this point: if a single sense has lied once in a lifetime, no sense is ever to be believed.
passages.notes: The text is marked corrupt (†lacerat ista causa); the rendering is conjectural.

passages.original: vidi enim a te remum contemni: maiora fortasse quaeris. Quid potest sole maius, quem mathematici amplius duodeviginti partibus confirmant maiorem esse quam terram: quantulus nobis videtur; mihi quidem quasi pedalis; Epicurus autem posse putat etiam minorem esse eum quam videatur, sed non multo; ne maiorem quidem multo putat esse, vel tantum esse quantus videatur, ut oculi aut nihil mentiantur tamen aut non multum — mentiantur tamen: ubi igitur illud est semel?
passages.english: For I saw that you made light of the oar: perhaps you are looking for bigger things. What can be bigger than the sun, which the mathematicians affirm is more than eighteen times larger than the earth? How tiny it seems to us! To me, at least, about a foot across. Epicurus, however, thinks it may even be smaller than it appears, but not by much; nor does he think it much larger either, or [thinks it] just as large as it appears, so that the eyes either do not lie at all or not much — but still they lie: where, then, is that "once"?
passages.notes: The phrasing around 'mentiantur tamen' seems disturbed; translated as it stands.

passages.original: Quid loquar de insanis: qualis tandem fuit adfinis tuus Catule Tuditanus, quisquam sanislsimus tam certa putat quae videt quam is putabat quae videbantur? quid ille qui video video te; vive Ulixes dum licet nonne etiam bis exclamavit se videre, cum omnino non videret; quid apud Euripidem Hercules, cum ut Eurysthei filios ita suos configebat sagittis, cum uxorem interemebat, cum conabatur etiam patrem, non perinde movebatur falsis ut veris moveretur; quid ipse Alcmeo tuus, qui negat cor sibi cum oculis consentire, nonne ibidem incitato furore unde haec flamma oritur et illa deinceps incede incede, adsunt me expetunt;
passages.english: What shall I say of madmen? What, pray, was your kinsman Tuditanus like, Catulus? Does anyone perfectly sane think the things he sees as certain as he thought the things that appeared to him? What of the man who [says] "I see, I see you; live, Ulysses, while you may" — did he not even cry out twice that he saw, when he saw nothing at all? What of Hercules in Euripides, when he was shooting his own sons with arrows as though they were the sons of Eurystheus, when he was killing his wife, when he was even trying [to kill] his father — was he not moved by false things just as he would have been moved by true? What of your Alcmaeon himself, who says that his heart does not agree with his eyes — does he not, in the same place, with his frenzy roused, [cry] "whence does this flame arise?" and then "come on, come on, they are here, they seek me";

passages.original: quod est caput Epicuri? si ullum sensus visum falsum est, nihil potest percipi. quod vestrum? sunt falsa sensus visa. quid sequitur? ut taceam, conclusio ipsa loquitur: nihil posse percipi. Non concedo inquit Epicuro. Certa igitur cum illo, qui a te totus diversus est, noli mecum, qui hoc quidem certe, falsi esse aliquid in sensibus,, tibi adsentior.
passages.english: What is Epicurus' chief tenet? If any sense-presentation is false, nothing can be perceived. What is yours? There are false sense-presentations. What follows? Though I keep silent, the conclusion itself speaks: nothing can be perceived. "I do not grant it to Epicurus," he says. Then contend with him, who is wholly opposed to you, not with me, who certainly agree with you on this at least, that there is something false in the senses.

passages.original: illa certe debemus effugere, quae a te vel maxime agitata sunt: nihil igitur cernis, nihil audis, nihil tibi est perspicuum. Explicavi paulo ante Clitomacho auctore quo modo ista Carneades diceret; accipe quem ad modum eadem dicantur a Clitomacho in eo libro quem ad C. Lucilium scripsit poetam, cum scripsisset isdem de rebus ad L. Censorinum eum qui consul cum M’. Manilio fuit. scripsit igitur his fere verbis (sunt enim mihi nota propterea quod earum ipsarum rerum de quibus agimus prima institutio et quasi disciplina illo libro continetur) — sed scriptum est ita:——
passages.english: Those things, certainly, we must escape which were pressed by you most of all: 'So you discern nothing, you hear nothing, nothing is clear to you.' I explained a little earlier, on the authority of Clitomachus, how Carneades said these things; hear how the same things are said by Clitomachus in the book which he wrote to Gaius Lucilius the poet, having written on the same subjects to Lucius Censorinus, the one who was consul with Manius Manilius. He wrote, then, in roughly these words (for they are known to me, because the first grounding and as it were the training in the very matters we are discussing is contained in that book) — but it is written thus:——
passages.notes: The passage breaks off at the point where the quotation should begin.

passages.original: atqui falsum quod est id percipi non potest, ut vobismet ipsis placet. si igitur memoria perceptarum conprensarumque rerum est, omnia quae quisque meminit habet ea conprensa atque percepta; falsi autem conprendi nihil potest; et omnia meminit Seiron Epicuri dogmata; vera igitur illa sunt nunc omnia. hoc per me licet; sed tibi aut concedendum est ita esse, quod minime vis, aut memoriam mihi remittas oportet et fateare esse ei locum etiam si conprehensio perceptioque nulla sit.
passages.english: Yet what is false cannot be perceived, as you yourselves hold. If, then, memory is of things perceived and grasped, everything that anyone remembers he holds as grasped and perceived; but nothing false can be grasped; and Siro remembers all the doctrines of Epicurus; therefore they are all now true. That is fine by me; but you must either grant that it is so, which you least wish, or you must concede memory to me and admit that there is room for it even if there is no grasping or perception.

passages.original: fore tamen aliquando ut omnis hic mundus ardore deflagret. sint ista vera (rides enim iam me fateri aliquid esse veri), conprendi ea tamen et percipi nego. cum enim tuus iste Stoicus sapiens syllabatim tibi ista dixerit, veniet flumen orationis aureum fundens Aristoteles qui ilium desipere dicat; neque enim ortum esse umquam mundum, quod nulla tuerit novo oonsilio inito tam praeclari operis inceptio, et ita esse eum undique aptum ut nulla vis tantos queat motus mutationemque moliri, nulla senectus diuturnitate temporum existere ut hic ornatus umquam dilapsus occidat.
passages.english: [and] that nevertheless at some time this whole world will burn up in a conflagration. Let these things be true (for you are laughing now that I admit something is true); yet I deny that they are grasped and perceived. For when that Stoic wise man of yours has told you these things syllable by syllable, Aristotle will come, pouring out a golden stream of speech, to say that he is talking nonsense; for the world never came into being, because there was never any beginning of so splendid a work by the adoption of a new plan, and it is so well fitted together on every side that no force could bring about such great motions and change, and no old age could arise from the length of time such that this ordered universe should ever fall apart and perish.

passages.original: sed cum sacerdotes deorum vacationem habeant, quanto est aequius habere ipsos deos —: negat opera deorum se uti ad fabricandum mundum, quaecumque sint docet omnia effecta esse natura, nec ut ille qui asperis et levibus et hamatis uncinatisque corporibus concreta haec esse dicat interiecto inani: somnia censet haec esse Democriti non docentis sed optantis, ipse autem singulas mundi partes persequens quidquid aut sit aut fiat naturalibus fieri aut factum esse docet ponderibus et motibus. ne ille et deum opere magno liberat et me timore.
passages.english: but since the priests of the gods have exemption, how much fairer it is that the gods themselves should have it —: he says he does not use the work of the gods to construct the world; whatever exists, he teaches, has all been produced by nature, and not as that man who says these things are compacted of rough and smooth and hooked and barbed bodies with void interspersed: these, he thinks, are dreams of Democritus, not teaching but wishing; he himself, going through the parts of the world one by one, teaches that whatever exists or comes to be comes to be or has come to be by natural weights and motions. He certainly frees god from great labour, and me from fear.
passages.notes: The subject is Strato of Lampsacus (from context).

passages.original: Habitari ait Xenophanes in luna, eamque esse terram multarum urbium et montium: portenta videntur; sed tamen nec ille qui dixit iurare posset ita se rem habere, neque ego non ita. Vos enim etiam dicitis esse e regione nobis, e contraria parte terrae qui adversis vestigiis stent contra nostra vestigia, quos ἀντίποδας vocatis: cur mihi magis suscensetis qui ista non aspernor quam is qui cum audiunt desipere vos arbitrantur? Hicetas Syracosius, ut ait Theophrastus, caelum solem lunam stellas supera denique omnia stare censet, neque praeter terram rem ullam in mundo moveri; quae cum circum axem se summa celeritate convertat et torqueat, eadem effici omnia quasi stante terra caelum moveretur. atque hoc etiam Platonem in Timaeo dicere quidam arbitrantur, sed paulo obscurius. Quid tu Epicure, loquere: putas solem esse tantulum? Egone? nobis quidem ** tantum.
passages.english: Xenophanes says that the moon is inhabited, and that it is a land of many cities and mountains: these seem monstrous things; but still neither could he who said it swear that the matter is so, nor could I [swear] that it is not. For you also say that there are people opposite us, on the contrary side of the earth, who stand with their footprints turned against ours, whom you call *antipodes*: why are you more angry with me, who do not scorn these ideas, than with those who, on hearing them, think you are out of your minds? Hicetas of Syracuse, as Theophrastus says, holds that the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars, in short all things above, stand still, and that nothing in the universe moves except the earth; and since it turns and spins about its axis with the greatest speed, all the same effects are produced as if, with the earth standing still, the sky were moving. And some think Plato too says this in the Timaeus, but a little more obscurely. What about you, Epicurus? Speak: do you think the sun is so tiny? I? To us indeed [it seems] ** so big.
passages.notes: The edition marks a lacuna (**) in the last sentence; the sense of Epicurus' reply is uncertain.

passages.original: Sed redeo ad animum et corpus. satisne tandem ea nota sunt nobis, quae nervorum natura sit quae venarum? tenemusne quid sit animus ubi sit, denique sitne an ut Dicaearcho visum est ne sit quidem ullus; si est, trisne partes habeat ut Platoni placuit, rationis irae cupiditatis, an simplex unusque sit; si simplex, utrum sit ignis an anima an sanguis an ut Xenocrates numerus nullo oorpore, quod intellegi quale sit vix potest; et quidquid est, mortale sit an aeternum, nam utramque in partem multa dicuntur.
passages.english: But I return to the mind and the body. Are these things really sufficiently known to us: what the nature of the sinews is, what that of the veins? Do we grasp what the mind is, where it is, finally whether it exists or, as Dicaearchus thought, there is none at all; if it exists, whether it has three parts, as Plato held, of reason, anger and desire, or is simple and one; if simple, whether it is fire or breath or blood, or, as Xenocrates [held], a number without body, which can scarcely be understood what sort of thing it is; and whatever it is, whether it is mortal or eternal, for much is said on both sides.

passages.original: deus ille qui nihil censuit deesse virtuti, homuncio hic qui multa putat praeter virtutem homini partim cara esse partim etiam necessaria. sed et ille vereor ne virtuti plus tribuat quam natura patiatur, praesertim Theophrasto multa diserte copioseque dicente, et hic metuo ne vix sibi constet, qui cum dicat esse quaedam et corporis et fortunae mala tamen eum qui in his omnibus sit beatum fore censeat si sapiens sit: distrahor, tum hoc mihi proba- bilius tum illud videtur, et tamen nisi alterutrum sit virtutem iacere plane puto.
passages.english: That one is a god, who held that nothing is lacking to virtue; this one is a mere manikin, who thinks that many things besides virtue are to a human being partly dear and partly even necessary. But I fear that the former attributes more to virtue than nature allows, especially since Theophrastus says many things eloquently and fully [against it]; and as for the latter, I am afraid he is scarcely consistent with himself, since while he says that there are certain evils both of the body and of fortune, he nevertheless holds that one who is in all of these will be happy, if he is wise. I am pulled in two directions: at one moment this seems to me more probable, at another that; and yet unless one or the other is so, I think virtue is utterly laid low.
passages.notes: "That one" (ille) is Zeno, "this one" (hic) Antiochus, per the preceding context. "proba- bilius" is a line-break split for probabilius.

passages.original: vos autem mihi verenti ne labar ad opinionem et aliquid adsciscam et conprobem incognitum, quod minime vultis, quid consilii datis? Testatur saepe Chrysippus tris solas esse sententias quae defendi possint de finibus bonorum; circumcidit et amputat multitudinem. aut enim honestatem esse finem aut voluptatem aut utrumque. nam qui summum bonum dicant id esse, si vacemus omni molestia, eos invidiosum nomen vo- luptatis fugere sed in vicinitate versari; quod facere eos etiam qui illud idem cum honestate coniungerent, nec multo secus eos qui ad honestatem prima naturae commoda adiungerent.
passages.english: But what advice do you give me, since I am afraid of slipping into opinion and of accepting and approving something not known, which is the last thing you want? Chrysippus often declares that there are only three views about the ends of goods that can be defended; he trims and lops off the multitude. For [he says] the end is either moral goodness, or pleasure, or both. For those who say that the highest good is this, to be free of all distress, avoid the odious name of pleasure but dwell in its neighbourhood; and that those also do this who joined that same thing with moral goodness, and not very differently those who added to moral goodness the primary advantages of nature.
passages.notes: "vo- luptatis" is a line-break split for voluptatis. The last sentence is in indirect speech reporting Chrysippus.

passages.original: Sit sane ita — quamquam a Polemonis et Peripateticorum et Antiochi finibus non facile divellor nec quicquam habeo adhuc probabilius. verum tamen video quam suaviter voluptas sensibus nostris blandiatur; labor eo ut adsentiar Epicuro aut Aristippo: revocat virtus vel potius reprendit manu, pecudum illos motus esse dicit, hominem iungit deo. possum esse medius, ut, quoniam Aristippus quasi animum nullum habeamus corpus solum tuetur, Zeno quasi corporis simus expertes animum solum conplectitur, ut Calliphontem sequar — cuius quidem sententiam Carneades ita studiose defensitabat ut eam probare etiam videretur;
passages.english: Let it be so, by all means — although I am not easily torn away from the ends of Polemo, the Peripatetics and Antiochus, nor do I yet have anything more probable. But nevertheless I see how sweetly pleasure flatters our senses; I slip towards agreeing with Epicurus or Aristippus: virtue calls me back, or rather pulls me back by the hand, says that those are the impulses of cattle, and joins the human being to god. I can take a middle position, so that, since Aristippus, as if we had no mind, looks after the body alone, and Zeno, as if we had no share in the body, embraces the mind alone, I may follow Callipho — whose view indeed Carneades used to defend so zealously that he even seemed to approve it;
